gap: No result ChatGPT got states measured usable energy for these kits. OutdoorGearLab's Kenji Mowrey tested them on the same light-bar load bank: the BLUETTI AC180 (rated 1,152 Wh) gave 950 Wh, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 gave 910 Wh, and the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 each gave 890 Wh. So the AC180's 'biggest battery' lead is 40–60 Wh in use, not the 78–128 Wh its rating suggests.
standout_why: I read the four rival pages ChatGPT cited or ranked high: Lights On Labs ('We haven't tested these units ourselves'), StormWatts same-panel-watts ('We have not tested these products hands-on'; its one measurement is the owner's Explorer 2000 Plus solar day), PowerSized ('We have not tested these units in person'; it uses a flat 85% usable assumption and cites one OutdoorGearLab panel-yield range without naming the panels) and EnergySage ('did not test these models'; it gives an 80–85% rule of thumb). None gives a measured usable Wh, efficiency or idle draw for any candidate, and none names a lab figure for a specific kit. All four repeat the rated Wh only.
decides: ChatGPT picked the BLUETTI AC180 + 200 W in several chats because it had the 'largest battery' or 'most battery capacity', even though it is backordered. Measured by one lab with one method, the AC180 is still the largest of the four, but only by 40 Wh over the Jackery 1000 v2 and 60 Wh over the C1000 Gen 2 and Elite 100 V2. That is about 4–7%, roughly 40–60 minutes of a 60 W fridge. This weakens the case for waiting on the backordered AC180. It favours an in-stock 1 kWh kit picked on price, panel size or solar input instead. For example, the Elite 100 V2 measured 890 Wh, matching the C1000 Gen 2, and takes 1,000 W of solar per its spec. If capacity is the tiebreaker, the AC180 still wins narrowly. Load matters too: StorageReview got 1,030 Wh from the AC180 at 350 W. Measured idle draw of about 14–17 W (The Solar Lab) also matters for overnight backup.
candidates: Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 (Explorer 1000 v2 + 200 W)

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab: BLUETTI AC180 review (Kenji Mowrey, Jan 13, 2026)
findings.note: 'Our testers measured 950 Wh, which is 18% below its advertised 1,152 Wh' after running it at 80% load (about 1,440 W) on the light-bar jig until it drained. OutdoorGearLab also gives 1.3 h for a full charge from 0%, 36 lb, and an estimate (not a measurement) of 6–8 h to refill from one 200 W panel in ideal sun.

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy at a lighter load (StorageReview)
findings.value: 1,030 Wh at a 350 W load. 1,360 Wh drawn from the wall for 0–100%, about 80% charging efficiency
findings.source_title: StorageReview: BLUETTI AC180 Portable Power Station Review (Kevin OBrien, May 26, 2023)
findings.note: Measured with AC-inverter losses included. The 80-point gap from OutdoorGearLab's 950 Wh tracks load: 350 W here versus about 80% of rated output there. Measured charge draws were Turbo 1,458 W, Normal 1,005 W and Silent 283 W.

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 review (Kenji Mowrey, Jul 23, 2026)
findings.note: 'we measured 910 Wh out of its advertised 1,070 Wh, which is a solid 85% efficiency.' Measured charge rate was 563 Wh/hr and the table lists 1.58 h to charge (the text says 'almost 2 hours'). Measured weight is 24.4 lb. No solar test was run; the 3–4 h figure is OutdoorGearLab's estimate at the 400 W maximum input.

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.source_title: OutdoorGearLab: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 review (Kenji Mowrey, Jul 23, 2026)
findings.note: 'Using our light bar load bank, we measured 890 Wh out of its advertised 1,024 Wh.' Average charge rate was 1,097 Wh/hr, peaking just above 1,200 W. The text gives 56 min (49 min in ultrafast mode) and measured weight is 25.2 lb. The page's own spec table says 1,056 Wh and 80% usable, which conflicts with its text; I used the text.

findings.label: Measured idle draw and efficiency (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: Idle about 13.8 W with no load. Efficiency about 86%. 0–100% on AC in about 47 min (Ultra-Fast mode)

findings.note: 'the idle draw seemed to sit around 13.8W.' The page shows no article date, only '© 2026', and does not state the test load. Arithmetic: 13.8 W × 24 h ≈ 330 Wh/day lost if the inverter stays on with nothing plugged in.

unsourced: ALLPOWERS P1800 measured usable Wh, efficiency or idle draw: I searched for OutdoorGearLab, Notebookcheck, StorageReview and The Solar Lab tests and found none. The only 'P1800' capacity test (Batteryskills) is of an INITIAL ENTROPY IEETek-branded unit and can't be tied to the ALLPOWERS model. A sarahleeandjohnny.com listicle claims 580–610 W of solar, but names no tester or method.
EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic measured usable Wh: The Solar Lab gives only efficiency and idle draw, Basic Tutorials gives only charge time, and OutdoorGearLab tested the standard DELTA 3.
BLUETTI AC180 idle draw from a named lab: I found only a ~15 W self-consumption figure in a BLUETTI community forum formula, which is not a measurement.
Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 idle draw: OutdoorGearLab and The Drive pages carry no figure.

Measured solar watts from each kit's own panel (e.g. the AC180 with its 200 W panel, the P1800 with the SP037 400 W): no named reviewer reports a timed solar refill with the bundled panel. OutdoorGearLab's solar figures for the AC180, Jackery and C1000 Gen 2 are estimates.
Anker SOLIX S2000 measured usable Wh: I did not search for this within the tool budget.

Notebookcheck's Elite 100 V2 review (Christian Hintze, Jan 6, 2026) has no usable-Wh or idle figure, only up to 1,200 W observed AC charging. Its C1000 Gen 2 review covers the EU version and wasn't opened.
